The European Commission indicated that individuals or companies affected by the anti-competitive practices revealed in this case could seek damages, leading several publishing groups to file lawsuits seeking a total of more than €640 million (approximately ¥118 billion). European publishers seek £552m+ from Google claiming ad market abuse - Press Gazette https://pressgazette.co.uk/marketing/european-publishers-seek-552m-from-google-claiming-ad-market-abuse/ Google sells ads on its websites and applications, acting as an intermediary between advertisers who want to place ads online and publishers (third-party websites and apps) who can provide ad space. Advertisers and publishers utilize digital tools from the ad tech industry to display real-time ads that are not linked to search queries, and Google offers several ad tech services that act as intermediaries between advertisers and publishers for ad placement on websites and mobile apps. In June 2023, the European Commission warned Google that it was distorting competition in the ad tech industry and violating antitrust laws. In response, Google proposed selling its ad tech business, but the proposal was rejected. Then, on September 5, 2025, local time, the European Commission stated that 'its own investigation has shown that Google holds a dominant position in the publisher ad server market with DFP, and in the open web programmatic ad buying tools market with Google Ads and DV360. Both markets cover the entire European Economic Area (EEA),' and announced that it would impose a fine of 2.95 billion euros (approximately 500 billion yen) on Google for violating antitrust laws in the ad tech market. Google fined over 500 billion yen by the EU for violating antitrust laws - GIGAZINE In its announcement that it would fine Google, the European Commission stated that 'any individual or company affected by anti-competitive conduct as described in this case may file a lawsuit in the courts of a Member State to seek damages. Even if the European Commission fines Google, national courts may order damages without deducting the European Commission's fine.' This means that damages suffered by individual companies will be considered separately from the fine imposed on Google by the European Commission. Therefore, more than 20 publishers from the Czech Republic, Estonia, France, Hungary, Finland, the Netherlands, Poland, and Sweden have jointly filed a lawsuit against Google seeking a total of 640 million euros (approximately 118 billion yen). In the lawsuit, they argue that 'if Google had not created a less competitive market, advertising revenue would have been much higher, and the cost of advertising technology services would have been much lower.' This lawsuit is being funded by Prague-based litigation financing firm LitFin, which has an agreement to cover the costs if they lose and receive a share of the compensation if they win. Matej Pardo, Chief Operating Officer of LitFin, said, 'The European Commission's final decision has determined that Google's abuse of its position across the entire advertising technology stack was illegal. Now is the time for publishers who have suffered damages as a result to receive compensation. By filing a class-action lawsuit, we can leverage economies of scale and enable small businesses across Europe to file similar lawsuits. Otherwise, it would be difficult to sue a financially powerful opponent like Google.' The U.S. Department of Justice has also ruled on Google's illegal monopoly in its advertising business, and in May 2025, a proposal was submitted to break up Google's major advertising-related businesses, arguing that Google had illegally acquired and maintained a monopolistic position in the advertising technology market. The Department of Justice has stated that Google should sell its advertising businesses, AdX and DFP, but Google is strongly protesting, calling it impossible - GIGAZINE In response, an American publisher filed a lawsuit against Google in January 2026, claiming that 'Google's advertising technology is deceptive and manipulative.' Google countered the allegations of monopoly by stating, 'These claims are unfounded. Advertisers and publishers have many options, and they choose Google's advertising technology tools because they are effective, affordable, and easy to use.'
